rationale: The later account explicitly recalls Alexander son of Philip as the Macedonian king who first ruled the Greeks, identifying the ruler introduced here.
Both accounts identify the accession of Antiochus called Epiphanes; 2 Maccabees places Jason's acquisition of the high priesthood at that transition.
The proposed covenant with surrounding nations reverses the law's prohibition of covenants with them and its warning that their worship would ensnare Israel.
The favourable reception of foreign customs corresponds to Jason's successful introduction of the Greek manner of life and displacement of lawful civic practices.
Both accounts connect the adoption of Greek institutions with royal permission, while 2 Maccabees names Jason and specifies his financial proposal.
Both accounts describe the establishment of a gymnasium in Jerusalem; 2 Maccabees locates it beneath the citadel and names Jason as its sponsor.
The reversal of circumcision is described as abandonment of the covenant; Genesis identifies circumcision in the flesh as its enduring sign.
The abandonment of ancestral covenantal identity corresponds to priests neglecting the altar and preferring Greek distinctions in the companion account.
Both accounts report Antiochus campaigning in Egypt; 2 Maccabees explicitly calls its expedition his second, so the two chronological presentations are not collapsed.
Both accounts connect Antiochus's movement from Egypt with an armed assault on Jerusalem; 2 Maccabees adds the report of revolt as his motive.
The king's intrusion into the sanctuary and seizure of sacred equipment correspond to the companion account of his profane entry and removal of the vessels.
The detailed list of stripped sanctuary furnishings expands the companion account's statement that Antiochus swept away sacred vessels and dedicated gifts.
The seizure of temple treasure corresponds to 2 Maccabees' report that Antiochus carried away eighteen hundred talents; the latter supplies an amount absent here.
Both accounts describe Antiochus's departure with temple wealth and characterize him by arrogance.
Mattathias and his sons' mourning gives a concrete household instance of the widespread grief following the devastation of Israel.

Both narratives describe a royal agent arriving with troops before a deceptive attack on Jerusalem; the titles and troop details differ, so this comparison does not equate the unnamed tribute collector with Apollonius.

Both narratives describe a commander feigning peace in Jerusalem before suddenly attacking its trusting inhabitants; 2 Maccabees adds the Sabbath setting. The unnamed tribute collector is not identified with Apollonius here.
The burning and demolition of Jerusalem provide the kind of destruction recalled in the companion account's prayer for the city being destroyed and levelled.
The capture of women and children corresponds to the royal order in 2 Maccabees to sell women and younger people, alongside the killing of adult men.
The fortified citadel established here remains a hostile base around the sanctuary and becomes the object of Judas's later siege.
The later appeal of the citadel's defenders and their lawless Israelite allies explains the continuing royal allegiance of the hostile garrison introduced here.
The armed and provisioned citadel described as a trap continues to support the nations and threaten the holy places, prompting Judas to besiege it.
The citadel's continuing hostility to Israel and the sanctuary is restated when its occupants hem Israel in around the holy places.
The companion account's prayer recalls both a profaned temple and innocent blood crying to God, the two injuries joined in this verse.
The later description of Jerusalem as deserted by its native inhabitants and occupied by foreigners resumes the displacement reported here.
The transformation of Sabbaths and festivals into occasions of reproach corresponds to the companion account's prohibition of Sabbath keeping and ancestral festivals.
Within the book, the city's honour turning into shame is reversed by the rededication's great gladness and removal of the nations' reproach.
Antiochus's demand for uniformity across his kingdom resembles Nebuchadnezzar's universal summons to common worship; these are distinct rulers and events.
The demand to abandon local customs corresponds to the royal mission to make Jews depart from ancestral and divine laws.
The Israelites' profanation of the Sabbath violates the command to remember and sanctify the seventh day.
The royal letters imposing foreign customs correspond to the companion narrative's royal agent charged with ending observance of ancestral laws.
The ban on Sabbath and festival observance is shared explicitly by the two accounts of religious persecution.

The suppression of sanctuary sacrifices corresponds to the prayer's lament that no burnt offering, sacrifice, incense, or place of offering is available; no identity of historical setting is asserted.
The command to defile the sanctuary corresponds to the companion account's dedication of Jerusalem's temple to Olympian Zeus.
The order to sacrifice pigs deliberately introduces an animal the law explicitly classifies as unclean and forbids Israel to eat.
The order to leave sons uncircumcised directly opposes the covenant requirement that every male be circumcised.
The stated aim of making Israel forget the law corresponds to the companion account's policy of compelling departure from God's laws.
Both accounts specify death for those who refuse the king's imposed Greek customs.
The expansion of compulsory sacrifice through royal administration corresponds to the decree extending coercion to neighbouring cities.
Those who abandon the law and join the royal policy become the lawless opponents against whom Mattathias's movement subsequently organizes resistance.
The later account identifies families seeking righteousness who withdraw into wilderness hiding places because of the persecution summarized here.
The later report to Antiochus explicitly recalls the abomination he built on Jerusalem's altar and announces its removal.

The death decree against possession of the covenant book or adherence to the law corresponds to the companion account's death penalty for refusing Greek customs; it does not separately attest the book searches.
The twenty-fifth-day sacrifice on the pagan altar supplies the desecration anniversary that the later rededication explicitly reverses.
Both accounts report women being executed because they circumcised their children.
Both accounts describe infants hung from the condemned women; 2 Maccabees specifies two women and their being thrown from the wall, whereas this account also mentions households and circumcisers.
Eleazar's refusal to eat pork provides a named example of the resistance to unclean food described collectively here.
The refusal of unclean food preserves the dietary boundary expressed in the law's prohibition of pork.
The seven brothers and their mother exemplify the declared choice of death rather than transgression of ancestral food laws.
The companion account interprets the disasters as God's disciplinary anger while also insisting that He has not abandoned His people.
Within the chapter, the initial naming of Simon prepares for Mattathias's later designation of this son as the brothers' counsellor and father.
The son introduced as Judas Maccabeus succeeds Mattathias as leader at the beginning of the next chapter.
The later battle account identifies Eleazar by the same epithet Avaran and recounts his death beneath an elephant.
The royal program of sanctuary defilement, idolatry, and suppression of the law identifies the blasphemies that prompt Mattathias's lament.
Mattathias's lament over a ruined holy city and sanctuary in foreign hands responds to the preceding account of bloodshed, foreign occupation, and desolation.
The lament's image of a dishonoured temple resumes the preceding description of the sanctuary's honour being turned into contempt.
The captive vessels of glory in Mattathias's lament are the sanctuary furnishings and treasures previously seized by Antiochus.
The lament over slain children and young men corresponds to the companion account's killing of people of every age during Jerusalem's sack.
The complaint about the nations seizing Jerusalem's spoils recalls the plundering of the city and storage of its spoils in the hostile citadel.
The lament that the city's adornment was removed recalls the literal stripping of the temple's crowns and gold ornament.
Mattathias's cry over profaned holy places summarizes the reported defilement and desolation of the sanctuary.
The sons later repeat the tearing of garments and great lament when they see the sanctuary's ruin before cleansing it.
The officials' arrival at Modein implements the earlier royal policy of sending overseers to compel sacrifice city by city.
The offer of royal friendship, wealth, and honour for abandoning ancestral worship resembles Antiochus's inducements to the youngest martyr; these are separate confrontations.
Mattathias's refusal to conform to royal worship parallels the three men's refusal to serve the king's idol despite a universal decree.
Mattathias's declaration that he and his family will remain in the ancestral covenant resembles Joshua's resolve that he and his household will serve the Lord despite others' choices.
Both declarations reject a king's demand on the explicit ground of obedience to the ancestral law.
Mattathias's refusal to turn right or left repeats the law's instruction to remain in the commanded way without deviation.
The man's public sacrifice at Modein is a concrete instance of the royal sacrifice policy and the cooperation of Israelites who abandoned the law.
Mattathias's zealous intervention follows the pattern of Phinehas rising to kill an offender before the assembly, a comparison made explicit two verses later.
Mattathias's demolition of the pagan altar corresponds to the command to pull down the nations' altars; this target does not prescribe the killing of the royal officer.

The verse explicitly invokes Phinehas's killing of Zimri; Numbers narrates the deed, names Zimri, and describes Phinehas's zeal. The paternal name is Salom here and Salu in Numbers; those forms are preserved.
The summons for everyone loyal to the covenant to gather after Mattathias echoes Moses' call for those belonging to the Lord to come to him during the golden-calf crisis.
Both accounts describe the resistance withdrawing into mountain wilderness; 2 Maccabees focuses on Judas and about nine companions rather than Mattathias's whole household.
The righteous families' withdrawal into the wilderness develops the earlier report that persecution drove Israel into places of refuge.
Families withdrawing with their children and livestock seek refuge from a campaign that had already captured women, children, and livestock and established an occupying citadel.
The king's forces in the city of David are situated in the fortified hostile base established in the preceding chapter.
Both accounts describe persecutors attacking Sabbath observers in hiding places; 2 Maccabees names Philip and burning, details not supplied in this account.
The offer of life for compliance restates the earlier royal decree imposing death on anyone who refuses the king's command.
The fugitives' refusal to profane the Sabbath appeals to the law sanctifying the seventh day; the law quoted here does not itself settle the later question of defensive fighting.
The attack on the hiding Sabbath observers corresponds to the companion narrative of cave dwellers killed while refraining from self-defence.
Both passages explicitly emphasize that reverence for the Sabbath restrained the victims from defending themselves.
The fugitives' choice to die in integrity resembles the martyrs' willingness to die rather than transgress ancestral law; the victims and circumstances remain distinct.
Both accounts recall the killing of nonresisting Sabbath observers in hiding places; the thousand lives and accompanying livestock are details specific to 1 Maccabees.
Within the chapter, Mattathias's community explicitly reasons from the massacre of the nonresisting families to the danger that repeating their course would destroy the whole movement.
The decision to fight defensively on the Sabbath responds to the kind of fatal refusal of self-defence commemorated in the companion account; it does not abolish Sabbath observance.
The gathering of volunteers devoted to the law resembles the companion account's assembly of those who had remained in Judaism, though the latter describes Judas's later recruitment.
The resistance grows as refugees join Mattathias; the companion account similarly describes Judas calling surviving adherents of Judaism into his company.

The armed action against lawless Israelites resembles the Levites' action against fellow Israelites during the golden-calf crisis; these distinct narratives connect covenant allegiance with internal judgment.
The campaign to pull down pagan altars follows the law's command to destroy the nations' places of worship and their altars.
The restoration of circumcision appeals to the covenant requirement for every male; Genesis supplies the obligation, not a separate authorization of the coercive means described here.
Judas continues Mattathias's successful pursuit of lawless opponents, with the next chapter describing their defeat and the removal of ungodliness from Judah.
The recovery of the law from foreign domination reverses the king's stated objective of making Israel forget the law and changing its ordinances.
Mattathias's deathbed description of a time of furious wrath recalls the narrator's earlier conclusion that very great wrath had come upon Israel.
The instruction to give one's life for the ancestral covenant is exemplified by the youngest martyr's declared surrender of body and soul for the ancestral laws.
Within Mattathias's speech, the general summons to remember ancestral deeds introduces the following named examples from Abraham through Daniel.
The statement that Abraham's faith was reckoned as righteousness reproduces the substance of Genesis' declaration about Abram.
The reference to Abraham being found faithful in testing recalls God's test involving Isaac and the recognition that Abraham feared God.
Joseph's keeping the commandment in distress is illustrated by his refusal to commit the sexual sin urged by his master's wife.
Pharaoh's appointment of Joseph over Egypt supplies the elevation recalled in Mattathias's summary of Joseph's life.
The everlasting priesthood granted for Phinehas's zeal is explicitly promised in the account of his intervention at Peor.
The summary of Joshua's leadership and obedience corresponds to his commission after Moses' death, with repeated commands to keep the law and lead Israel into its inheritance.
Caleb recalls his faithful report despite the other spies and receives Hebron as his inheritance, the two features joined in Mattathias's summary.
The enduring royal throne recalls God's promise to establish David's house and his descendant's throne for ever; the promise supplies the dynastic outcome summarized here.
Elijah's repeated profession that he was most zealous for the Lord supplies the zeal for the law recalled in this verse.
Elijah's being taken up is narrated at his separation from Elisha, when the fiery chariot appears and he is taken up as into heaven.
Daniel's account explicitly names Hananiah, Azariah, and Mishael and says that they were preserved when the furnace flame killed their captors.
The angel's removal of the furnace flame and the fire's failure to harm the companions narrate the rescue remembered here.
God shuts the lions' mouths, and Daniel attributes his rescue to righteousness found in him, matching both integrity and deliverance in the summary.
Mattathias's confidence that those who hope in God will not fail resembles the companions' prayer that those trusting in Him will not be put to shame.

The companion account later portrays the proud Antiochus brought low with worms and bodily decay, illustrating the warning about a sinful ruler's passing glory without making it a predictive identification.
The warning that the ruler returns to dust and his thought perishes closely resembles the psalm's warning that a ruler returns to earth and his reasonings perish.
The instruction to be courageous and strong in the law recalls Joshua's commission, which joins courage, careful obedience, and prospering in the commanded way.
The later assembly chooses Simon to lead in place of Judas and Jonathan and follow his commands, developing the responsibility Mattathias assigns him here.
Judas's succession and the brothers' support show the implementation of Mattathias's designation of him as military commander.
The instruction to gather those who keep the law corresponds to the companion account's description of Judas recruiting those who had remained in Judaism.

Mattathias's blessing of his sons and being gathered to his fathers recalls Jacob's final blessing of his sons and being gathered to his people; this is a deathbed pattern, not an identity of speakers.
The later account of Simon's family monument at Modein recalls Mattathias's burial there and includes the father among the commemorated family members.
Judas's succession carries out Mattathias's explicit designation of him as the brothers' army commander.
Those who had joined Mattathias are the law-devoted warriors and refugees whose gathering was narrated in the previous chapter.
The opening portrait of Judas armed for battle develops his father's description of him as a strong warrior appointed to command the army.

The portrait of Judas as a lion resembles the companion account's description of his men rushing upon the enemy like lions; the comparison concerns martial imagery rather than the identity of battles.
The pursuit and burning of opponents correspond to the companion account's summary of Judas's unexpected attacks and burning of hostile settlements.
Both accounts portray Judas's growing success in putting hostile forces to flight and associate that success with deliverance for Israel.
Both summaries connect Judas's successful campaign through settlements with a change from divine anger to mercy or deliverance for Israel.
The companion account likewise joins Judas's gathering of endangered adherents of Judaism with the spread of his military reputation.
Judas's taking and keeping his defeated opponent's sword resembles David's appropriation of Goliath's weapon and equipment; Apollonius and Goliath remain distinct opponents.
Seron's report about Judas's assembly of faithful warriors follows the gathering of those devoted to the law around Mattathias's family.
Within the chapter, Seron's ambition to gain a name and royal honour by defeating Judas is answered by his army's defeat and flight.
The troops' alarm at a more numerous force is the situation addressed by the law's instruction not to fear a larger enemy army.
Judas's assertion that Heaven can save by many or few closely echoes Jonathan's declaration that the Lord is not constrained from saving by many or few.
The claim that military strength comes from heaven rather than army size echoes David's assertion that the battle belongs to the Lord and salvation does not depend on weapons.
Within the chapter, the feared destruction and dispossession of Israel is spelled out in Antiochus's later orders to remove its remnant and allot the land to foreigners.
The defence of life and ancestral customs corresponds to the companion account's description of Judas preparing men to die for the laws and homeland.
Judas's assurance that God will crush the enemy and his command not to fear resemble the law's battle exhortation that God fights with Israel to save it.
Both accounts describe news of Judas's successes reaching governing authorities and prompting the dispatch of stronger forces.
The royal mobilization against Judas corresponds to the companion account's appeal for assistance and dispatch of Nicanor and Gorgias; the administrative sequence is presented differently.
The narrator's explanation that abolishing ancestral customs caused the kingdom's troubles is later acknowledged when peace is proposed by restoring those customs.
Antiochus's decision to seek eastern wealth is followed by his attempt to seize the rich temple of Elymais in Persia.
The companion account likewise presents Lysias as the king's guardian and chief minister; this identifies his governmental role without equating the surrounding campaigns.
Lysias's assignment to bring up Antiochus's son explains the later notice that he had raised the son from youth and installed him as king.
Within the chapter, Lysias implements his charge over the forces by selecting commanders and sending them against Judah according to the king's command.
Both accounts state that the dispatched force was intended to eradicate the people of Judea.
The plan to resettle foreigners in Israel resembles Lysias's later stated intention to make Jerusalem a Greek dwelling; the passage in 2 Maccabees occurs under a different narrative setting.
Antiochus's journey to the upper countries has its corresponding eastern setting in the companion account's notice of his retreat from Persia.
Both accounts associate Ptolemy with the selection of Nicanor and Gorgias against Judea, while 1 Maccabees places the selection under Lysias and 2 Maccabees gives Ptolemy the active role.

Both accounts describe the force sent with Nicanor and Gorgias to destroy Judea, but the reported strengths differ: forty thousand men plus seven thousand cavalry here, and no fewer than twenty thousand men there.
The enemy encampment near Emmaus becomes the camp Judas deliberately attacks while Gorgias's detachment is away.
Both accounts describe merchants preparing to buy Jewish captives before the battle; 2 Maccabees adds Nicanor's proposed price and plan to pay the Roman tribute.
Both accounts describe Judas learning that the royal force was advancing against his people before he prepares the defenders.
The call to fight for the people and holy places corresponds to Judas's exhortation to remember the outrages against the sanctuary, city, and ancestral order.
Both accounts describe the resistance collectively seeking divine rescue before battle and appealing beyond their own strength.
The description of deserted Jerusalem, a trampled sanctuary, and foreign occupation recalls the establishment of the citadel and the inhabitants' flight.
Samuel's gathering of Israel at Mizpah for prayer and fasting supplies the earlier use of Mizpah as a place of prayer explicitly recalled here.
The renewed fast at Mizpah recalls the earlier national fast at the same place under Samuel; the sackcloth and ashes are additional features of the present assembly.
Both preparations for battle include use of the sacred book, here unrolled at the prayer assembly and there read aloud before engagement.
The Nazirites who have completed their days require the sanctuary offerings prescribed at completion of a vow, explaining why the sanctuary's profanation creates a practical crisis.
The question where to take the offerings resembles the prayer's lament over the absence of a place to offer gifts and its appeal for acceptance despite that loss.
Both prayers ask God to look upon the sanctuary's profanation and the suffering of His people.
The prayer's report that nations have gathered to destroy Israel corresponds to the companion account's stated purpose of Nicanor's multinational force.
The confession that Israel cannot stand without God's help corresponds to Judas's contrast between reliance on weapons and reliance on the Almighty.
The assembly's trumpet signal and cry to Heaven fit the law's provision of trumpet signals in defensive war so that Israel may be remembered and delivered before God.
The hierarchy of thousands, hundreds, fifties, and tens repeats the divisions established under Moses, here adapted to military leadership.
The four exemptions for a house, vineyard, betrothal, and fear correspond directly to the law that the verse says Judas followed.
The Jewish encampment south of Emmaus prepares for Judas's movement against the king's camp there in the following account.
The summons to courage before battle resembles the law's exhortation against fear when Israel faces its enemies with God's help.
Judas's preference for death in defence of the nation and holy places corresponds to the companion account's description of men ready to die for the laws and homeland.
Gorgias's detached force belongs to the army of selected commanders dispatched by Lysias in the preceding chapter.
Judas targets the royal camp at Emmaus, the location established when the invading force entered the land.
Within the battle narrative, Gorgias's assumption that Judas's men are fleeing is reversed when his returning detachment sees the ruined camp and itself flees.
Judas's poorly equipped force recalls the earlier crisis of few and exhausted defenders, answered by his insistence that victory depends on heavenly strength.
The sight of a large force with cavalry is precisely the battle situation in which the law tells Israel not to fear.
Judas's command not to fear a numerous attacking army closely follows the law's exhortation to courage before a stronger enemy.
The explicitly recalled rescue at the Red Sea is narrated when Pharaoh's pursuing army enters the sea, is overwhelmed, and Israel is saved.
Both prebattle petitions seek rescue on the basis of the covenants with the fathers rather than confidence in Israel's own resources.
The expectation that the nations will learn who saves Israel resembles David's declaration that victory will make all the earth know there is a God in Israel.
The trumpet sounded as Judas's men enter battle corresponds to the law's signal for defensive war and appeal to be remembered before God.
Both accounts describe Judas's men defeating the invading force and forcing it to flee; the detailed tactical sequence and casualty totals differ.
Both accounts include slaughter and pursuit after the invaders' defeat, but the three thousand reported here differs from the companion account's more than nine thousand.
Both accounts describe the victors returning from pursuit; 2 Maccabees explicitly gives the approaching Sabbath as its reason, whereas this narrative turns to Gorgias's remaining force.
Within the battle account, Judas's instruction to delay plunder is followed by the taking of the camp's wealth after the remaining threat has fled.
The warning about Gorgias's nearby detachment explains why the army remains ready until that detachment appears and flees, after which plunder begins.
The retreat of Gorgias's men reverses his earlier claim that Judas's men were the ones fleeing.
Both accounts describe the victorious Jews taking enemy wealth and equipment after the force that threatened them has been defeated.
The thanksgiving that God's mercy is for ever reproduces the refrain of the psalm's opening summons to give thanks for His kindness.
The companion account also interprets the victory as the Lord preserving His people and granting them a beginning of mercy.
Reports of the defeated armies first reach Lysias here and later reach Antiochus, who is told also of Lysias's own defeat.
Lysias's distress that the king's commands failed refers back to his commission to destroy Israel's strength and replace its population.
Both accounts describe Lysias assembling a large force after distressing news; the troop totals and narrative chronology differ, so the campaigns are compared without being equated.
Both accounts place a campaign of Lysias at Beth-zur, although the surrounding chronology and military figures differ.
Judas's prayer expressly remembers David's defeat of the mighty man, narrated when David strikes Goliath with the stone and kills him with his own sword.
The second example in the prayer is Jonathan and his armour-bearer's attack on the foreign station, followed by terror from the Lord.
The prayer that the enemy army be delivered into Israel's hand repeats the assurance in David's battle speech that the Lord will hand the foreigners over.
The request for the enemy's courage to collapse develops the terror from the Lord in Jonathan's victory, the episode explicitly recalled two verses earlier.
Both prayers ask God to crush the oppressors' strength and make His name known and glorified through the rescue of His servants.
Both accounts describe Lysias's force being defeated and fleeing, but the casualty figures differ and their narrative settings are not assumed identical.
Both narratives describe Lysias withdrawing after defeat; 1 Maccabees emphasizes renewed recruitment, while 2 Maccabees describes an ensuing attempt at negotiation.
The resolve to cleanse and rededicate the holy places corresponds to the companion account of Judas recovering and purifying the temple.
The gathering at Mount Zion corresponds to the companion account's recovery of the temple and city by Maccabeus and his companions.
The condition Judas's army sees at the sanctuary confirms the earlier report of its defilement and wilderness-like desolation.
The burned sanctuary gates correspond to the companion account's mention of those who had set fire to the sacred gateways.
The tearing of garments and great lament at the sanctuary repeat the mourning of Mattathias and his sons over the original devastation.

Both accounts describe prostration and appeal to Heaven in connection with the temple's restoration; here it precedes cleansing, while the companion account places its prayer after the renewed offerings.
The order to contain the citadel's forces while the temple is cleansed addresses the continuing ambush against the sanctuary established in the earlier account.
Both accounts explicitly describe the purification of the temple before its worship is restored.
The deliberation over the defiled altar leads to the replacement altar also reported in the companion account.
The dismantling of the profaned altar explains the companion account's brief statement that another altar was made after purification.
Deferring the decision about sacred stones until a prophet comes resembles the later provision that Simon's settlement should stand until a trustworthy prophet arises.
The use of whole stones according to the law directly corresponds to the instruction to build an altar of whole stones untouched by iron.
The requirement to use whole stones is reinforced by the prohibition of hewn altar stones, because a blade would defile them.
The rebuilding and consecration of the holy places corresponds to the companion account's concise description of temple purification and restoration of worship.
The new lampstand, incense altar, and table replace the specific sanctuary furnishings Antiochus had taken away.
The provision of new vessels enables the renewed incense, lamps, and loaves named together in the companion account.
The relighting of the temple lamps restores the ordinance of maintaining the lamps on the pure lampstand before the Lord.
Both restoration accounts explicitly name the offering of incense and the lighting of lamps.
The return of loaves to the table restores the prescribed arrangement of bread before the Lord.
Both accounts include setting out the loaves among the renewed acts of sanctuary worship.
Both accounts date the purification or rededication to the twenty-fifth of Chislev; the Seleucid year is supplied here.
The renewed whole burnt offerings on the stone altar correspond to the law's instruction to offer whole burnt offerings upon the altar of whole stones.
Both accounts describe sacrifices being offered on a newly made altar after the sanctuary's purification.
The dedication anniversary explicitly answers the earlier sacrifice on the pagan altar on the twenty-fifth day.
Both accounts emphasize that purification occurred on the same day of the month as the temple's desecration.
Both restoration narratives describe the people falling on their faces after worship has been renewed.
Both accounts praise the One who made the sanctuary's purification prosper, although the companion account also mentions branches and palm fronds.
Both accounts describe eight joyful days celebrating the restoration; 2 Maccabees compares the celebration to the Festival of Booths.
The renewed golden crowns on the temple front answer the earlier removal of its crowns and gold ornament.
The people's great gladness and removal of reproach reverse the earlier turning of the sanctuary's festivals and glory into mourning and dishonour.
Both accounts describe a communal decree establishing annual observance of the days of dedication.
John later places Jesus in Jerusalem at the Feast of Dedication, providing a subsequent setting for the festival whose annual observance is instituted here.
The later report to Antiochus specifically recalls the high walls erected around the restored sanctuary.
The later appeal to the king confirms that the sanctuary and Beth-zur had both been fortified, the protective works described here.
